P1.evidence: No setter code and no application referenced, so the read-back does not apply. The usual three-part frame: 'it's just an opportunity for me to understand where you are today. Where do you want to be? If we can help, I can show you some options, okay?' — 'what's in the way' omitted again, which on a prospect whose entire self-diagnosis is about what gets in the way was the element worth having. Agreement was the trailing 'okay'. The open question ran cleanly. Note the call lost its first six minutes to a camera failure and the rep flagged the time pressure himself: 'we have a limited amount of time. Let's dive straight into it.'

P2.evidence: Announced and part-run: 'Let's get a bit of a baseline for yourself.' The training week was properly elicited — 'What is your current training regimen?' — and produced a full six-session breakdown. Occupation was asked directly and its physical nature explored: 'And what is it that you do for work, Fred?' Energy was asked and returned the diet numbers. Age is inferred rather than asked; height and weight were never obtained at all, on a call where the primary goal is body composition. The clinical checks are both misses and one of them matters: the prospect named injury as his single biggest risk at 00:09:00 and mentioned a back injury from calisthenics that put him out, and neither drew a question. Diet scores a partial because the rep engaged with the numbers when they were volunteered — 1,300 to 1,400 calories, 170 g protein, no carbs — and later asked about supplements, but never asked what he eats. Sleep was not raised at all in a 49-year-old training six times a week in a steep deficit.

P3.evidence: Good persistence against a resistant prospect. The rep pushed the why four separate times — 'why are you not comfortable being average?', 'But why?', 'So do you feel like you look average at the moment?' — through a wall of 'I don't know' and 'it's a vanity thing', and eventually broke through to the real material. The who-else move was the turning point: 'You also mentioned you have a missus... How do you want to show up for her?' followed by 'Why is that important for you to be a role model to your boys?', which produced the most honest passage of the call — three sons, an eldest who struggles to stay fit, and 'I want to show him that it can be done at 50.' The work-ripple attempt at 00:22:45 failed and was pushed twice more before the prospect flatly closed it: 'It's not really going to affect my work too much.' The reflect-back never came. Nothing in the shape of 'so this isn't really about the summer, it's about showing your boys — is that right?' was ever said, and that sentence would have been the strongest asset available when price landed twenty minutes later.

P4.evidence: The strongest phase on the call. Past attempts and outcomes were both drawn out — calisthenics until 'I hurt my back and I was out of it for a while and then I started running' — and the root-cause question ran with the mentor framing: 'what has kept you stuck in the past will keep you stuck in the future somehow... what has kind of come up for you that makes you not actually take action?' The self-sufficiency challenge produced the single most valuable sentence in this entire folder: asked 'What's the rationale on getting outside help as opposed to ChatGPT, YouTube, Instagram?', the prospect answered 'I'm 100% confident I can build myself a program-ish, but I can't tell if I'm doing it right. I don't want to injure myself.' That is the value proposition articulated by the buyer, unprompted, and it names precisely which component he will pay for. The gap-naming scores only a partial because he could not identify the obstacle himself — 'I don't even know what the obstacles has been' — and the rep did not name it for him.

P5.evidence: No consequence was built and no line was drawn. The settle-for framing appeared as an observation rather than a question — 'I don't get a sense from you, Fred, that you're comfortable being average' — and the why-not was pursued well and repeatedly, which is the one check that lands. But there is no cost-of-inaction question anywhere, and no line in the sand. The prospect handed over a ready-made deadline and it was never used: he said 'I'm going to be 50 next year', 'time is running out', 'it's now or never', and '50 is the deadline. I just said it for myself.' A man who has set his own hard date twelve months out is asking to be closed against it, and the rep asked why the deadline mattered instead of what happens if he misses it.

P6.evidence: The trust gauge was run and never answered. Asked to put himself on the one-to-ten, the prospect deflected — 'It's one of these things where I don't think I will know until I get [there]' — and no number was ever obtained. The rep followed up on the reasoning rather than on the number and moved on. The capability check then produced a self-sufficiency statement, not a yes: 'I get a feeling I'm going to make it happen regardless. If I can make it happen better and quicker.' That is a man saying he does not need the programme, and he had said it once already at 00:25:29 — 'It's happening regardless.' The all-in question was never asked. Price was presented against an unanswered gauge and two explicit statements of independence, and it was rejected inside ninety seconds.

P11.evidence: An explicit refusal on value ended the call, so payment, the Trevor booking, the agreement and onboarding were all unreachable.

objection_plays.detail: One move ran and it was the best-executed single move in this batch. On 'that's way out of what I would want to spend', the rep asked 'Is it a case of not being able to spend that or you just don't feel like it's worth that?' That is the isolation the script demands and it is the only time in twelve calls that anyone separates capacity from value. It returned an unambiguous answer — 'Oh, it's 100% not worth that to me' — which correctly told the rep that the open-wallet play does not apply here, since none of the financial-picture questions help a prospect who can pay and will not. Scored partial rather than hit because the rest of the play never ran and because, having correctly diagnosed a value objection, the rep had nothing to switch to.

SCRIPT GAP — 'I can get that way cheaper than that', fourth instance in this batch and the purest statement of it in the corpus. This is the gap already logged in playbook.json against the Badrane Hriouch call, and it has now appeared with Hamdi Hmimy, Kyle Loftus, Andreas Xagoraris and here, four times in five days from one rep. The prospect's benchmark is explicit and unusually informative: he has paid a professional gun dog trainer for exactly this delivery model — film it, send it, get critique back — and got 'very good results' from it. He is pricing $4,000 against what remote video critique costs in every other domain he has bought it in. There is nothing scripted for this and the rep folded within one turn: 'I'm not going to try and convince you otherwise.' Building a value play for a proven-cheaper-substitute should be the single highest priority in the playbook.

SCRIPT GAP — the buyer who wants one component. He specified the scope himself and could not have been clearer: 'I'm 100% confident I can build myself a program-ish, but I can't tell if I'm doing it right' and 'the kettlebells section of it, I'm a complete novice at it.' He does not want programming, does not want nutrition, and explicitly does not want motivation — he has already decided. He wants form critique on kettlebells. Third occurrence of the unbundling gap in this batch after Hamdi Hmimy and Kyle Loftus, and there is still no tier between $200/mo and $4,000 that sells it.

SCRIPT GAP — the prospect whose resolve is already maximal. 'I've already decided, mate. It's not a want or... It's happening regardless' and later 'I get a feeling I'm going to make it happen regardless.' The entire process from Phase 3 through Phase 6 is engineered to manufacture resolve and then sell against it; when the resolve pre-exists, the script has nothing left to trade. To his credit the rep tested it with a takeaway — 'Just follow that, continue to make progress in that way' — which correctly surfaced the kettlebell gap, but there is no scripted route from there to a close. Worth noting because these prospects are not low-intent, they are simply not buying motivation.

Fear of injury was raised early and unprompted — 'my biggest risk to reaching my goals, I feel, is injury, and trying too hard' — with a concrete history behind it: he hurt his back doing calisthenics and lost weeks, and described the relapse spiral that follows. The rep did not engage with it when it landed but did address it later and well, tying the film-and-review loop to the prospect's own gun dog experience: 'it's the same thing that you did with your dog trainer, essentially.' None of the scripted moves ran — no certainty question, no BRIDGE, no PLANE, and no BURNED BEFORE, which was directly applicable.

notes: Phase 4 here is the best in the folder and produced the clearest statement of the value proposition anyone gives in this corpus: this buyer will pay for form critique and nothing else. The call was then lost in three specific places. First, the trust gauge was left unanswered and price was presented against two explicit statements that he will succeed regardless — that is not a clear yes and the script says do not proceed. Second, the prospect supplied his own hard deadline, his fiftieth birthday twelve months out, and no consequence was ever built against it. Third, and outside the rep's control, once he correctly diagnosed a value objection rather than an affordability one there was no play to switch to, and the $1,200 trial he offers as a matter of course in four other calls this week was not offered here. The isolating question at 00:45:07 is exemplary and should be taught.
